x.text: AI is already helping build the next generation of AI. The question isn't whether recursive self-improvement happens. It's who's checking the work while it does.

We're building machines that do more of our thinking for us, then acting surprised when people treat them as more than a tool. The real risk may be less about machines becoming gods and more about humans deciding they don't need to think for themselves.
If AI can discover mathematical truths that humans couldn't find, does understanding the proof become less important? Or does it become more important than ever?

We're approaching a world where knowing how to use an application matters less than knowing what an agent is allowed to do inside it. That's a much bigger shift than a new way to interact with software.

linkedin.text: It doesn't have to be conscious to be dangerous. We may be spending too much time debating whether AI is becoming sentient and not enough time examining what happens when increasingly capable systems can influence people, shape decisions, and take actions in the real world. The consequences don't depend on whether there's anyone home inside the machine.

AI governance is going to be as much a geopolitical challenge as a technical one. Countries aren't going to stop developing capabilities because of international agreements. Building enough transparency and mutual trust to make those capabilities less dangerous is a much more realistic starting point.

We're moving from software people operate to software their agents operate. That's a pretty fundamental change in how applications need to be designed. The interface might become optional, but permissions, security and accountability certainly aren't.

National security is moving out of the government relations department and into the boardroom. When your products are foundational to global AI infrastructure, export controls, geopolitical exposure, and commercial strategy become deeply interconnected. That's a different kind of corporate governance challenge.
